key_terms.meaning: A set V of vertices and a set E of edges, each edge joining two vertices (or one vertex, for a loop).
The number of edge-ends at vertex v; a loop counts twice, and Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.
The simple graph on n vertices in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge; it has n(n−1)/2 edges.
A graph whose vertex set splits into two parts so that every edge goes from one part to the other.
A graph in which every vertex has the same degree; k-regular means every degree equals k.
An n×n matrix with aᵢⱼ = number of edges between vᵢ and vⱼ; entry (i,j) of Aᵏ counts walks of length k from vᵢ to vⱼ.
For each vertex, a list of its neighbours; storage is O(|V| + |E|), good for sparse graphs.
An |V|×|E| matrix whose column for edge e has 1s in the two rows of its endpoints.
A bijection f: V₁ → V₂ such that {u,v} is an edge of G₁ exactly when {f(u), f(v)} is an edge of G₂.
A walk in which no vertex repeats; its length is the number of edges it uses.
A trail is a walk with no repeated edge; a circuit is a closed trail, that is, one that starts and ends at the same vertex.
A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph; a cut vertex is a vertex whose removal does.
A maximal set of vertices that are all reachable from one another; a graph is connected when it has exactly one component.
A closed trail that uses every edge of the graph exactly once; it exists exactly when the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree.
A cycle that visits every vertex of the graph exactly once and returns to the start.
For a connected planar graph drawn without crossings, |V| − |E| + |F| = 2, where F counts faces including the outer one.
The least number of colours needed to colour the vertices so that adjacent vertices get different colours.
If d[u] + w(u,v) < d[v], replace d[v] by d[u] + w(u,v); the smallest tentative distance is always final.
A connected graph with no cycle; on n vertices it always has exactly n − 1 edges.
A spanning tree of a weighted connected graph whose total edge weight is as small as possible.

takeaways: A graph is just two sets, V and E; almost every later idea is a property of those two sets.
Matrix and list representations trade memory against speed, so the right choice depends on whether the graph is dense or sparse.
Isomorphism asks whether two drawings are the same graph with the labels rubbed out; degree sequence and cycle structure are the first tests to try.
Connectivity is about reachability: paths, components, bridges and cut vertices all measure how easily a network falls apart.
Euler conditions are about edges and are easy to check (all degrees even); Hamiltonian conditions are about vertices and are hard (NP-complete).
Planarity is a drawing question, and Euler's formula converts it into counting, which proves K₅ and K₃,₃ cannot be drawn flat.
Colouring models conflicts; χ(G) ≤ Δ + 1 always, and χ(G) = 2 exactly for bipartite graphs with at least one edge.
Dijkstra's algorithm is correct only for non-negative weights, and its running time depends on the priority queue used.
A tree is the cheapest possible connected graph: connected with n − 1 edges, acyclic, or unique paths between all pairs.
Greedy MST algorithms (Kruskal and Prim) are provably optimal because of the cut property of minimum weight edges.
bank_note: Long answers here are graded on structure: a precise definition, a small labelled example or counterexample, the statement of the theorem you use, a proof or proof sketch, and the algorithm with its complexity.

bank.q: Define a simple graph, a multigraph and a pseudograph. State and prove the handshaking lemma, and deduce that a simple graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices.
outline: Formal definitions with V and E, loops and parallel edges distinguished.
Handshaking lemma: each edge contributes 2 to the degree sum, so Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.
Counting odd-degree vertices modulo 2 gives an even count.
Example: a 3-regular graph on 6 vertices has 9 edges.
Corollary: no simple graph can have exactly one odd-degree vertex.

bank.q: Explain the adjacency matrix, adjacency list and incidence matrix representations of a graph. Compare them on memory use and on the time to answer 'are u and v adjacent?'
outline: Adjacency matrix definition, symmetry for undirected graphs, diagonal for loops.
Adjacency list definition; total storage O(|V| + |E|).
Incidence matrix with one column per edge and two 1s per column.
Dense graph: matrix is fine, O(1) adjacency test. Sparse graph: list wins on memory.
Note Aᵏ[i][j] counts walks of length k.

bank.q: Define graph isomorphism. Give two non-isomorphic graphs with the same number of vertices, edges and degree sequence, and prove they are not isomorphic.
outline: Bijection definition with the edge-preserving condition both ways.
Invariants: number of vertices, edges, degree sequence, number and lengths of cycles, number of components.
Counterexample: a 6-cycle versus two disjoint triangles — both 2-regular on 6 vertices, 6 edges.
Distinguish them by number of connected components or girth.
Conclusion: invariants can disprove isomorphism but a matching invariant list does not prove it.

bank.q: State the equivalent characterisations of a tree on n vertices and prove that any two of them imply the others.
outline: List: connected and acyclic; connected with n − 1 edges; acyclic with n − 1 edges; unique simple path between every pair; adding any edge creates exactly one cycle.
Induction on n using a leaf (every tree with n ≥ 2 has at least two leaves).
Removing a leaf gives a smaller tree, giving the edge count.
Uniqueness of paths follows from acyclicity; a cycle would give two paths.
Small example: n = 4 gives 4 non-isomorphic labelled trees' shapes, 16 labelled trees by Cayley's formula.

bank.q: Define Euler path, Euler circuit, Hamiltonian path and Hamiltonian cycle. State the necessary and sufficient condition for an Euler circuit and an Euler path, and give a sufficient condition for a Hamiltonian cycle.
outline: Definitions of trail, circuit, path and cycle restated precisely.
Euler circuit: connected (ignoring isolated vertices) and every degree even.
Euler path but no circuit: exactly two odd-degree vertices, which become the endpoints.
Hamiltonian sufficient condition: Dirac's theorem, deg(u) + deg(v) ≥ n for every non-adjacent pair, or deg(v) ≥ n/2 for all v.
Contrast: Euler is a condition on degrees, Hamiltonian has no known simple necessary and sufficient test.

bank.q: Run Dijkstra's algorithm on a weighted undirected graph of your choice with 6 vertices and non-negative weights. Show the distance table after each iteration and give the final shortest path tree.
outline: Initialise d[s] = 0, all others ∞, settled set empty.
Each iteration: pick the unsettled vertex of least d, settle it, relax its neighbours.
Table of d-values after each step, with the parent pointer for each vertex.
Final shortest distances and the shortest path tree edges.
Complexity: O((|V| + |E|) log |V|) with a binary heap.

bank.q: For a weighted connected graph with at least 6 vertices and 9 edges, find a minimum spanning tree by Kruskal's algorithm and again by Prim's algorithm. Show that both give the same total weight.
outline: Sort edges by weight; add an edge if it does not create a cycle (union-find check).
Prim: start at a vertex, repeatedly add the cheapest edge leaving the grown tree.
Full edge list at each step with accept/reject reasons.
Both totals equal; MST is not unique when weights tie.
Complexity: Kruskal O(|E| log |E|), Prim O(|E| log |V|) with a heap.

bank.q: A connected planar graph has 10 vertices and every face is bounded by a cycle of length 4 or more. Use Euler's formula to find the maximum possible number of edges, and draw a graph that attains it.
outline: Euler: |V| − |E| + |F| = 2.
Face-edge count: 2|E| = Σ (length of face) ≥ 4|F|, so |F| ≤ |E|/2.
Substitute: 10 − |E| + |E|/2 ≥ 2, giving |E| ≤ 16.
Note the general bound |E| ≤ 3|V| − 6 for simple planar graphs with |V| ≥ 3.
Example attaining it: the cube graph plus a diagonal pair, or any 4-regular planar graph of the right size.

bank.q: Find the chromatic number of a cycle Cₙ, a complete graph Kₙ and a bipartite graph. Then colour a given graph with 7 vertices using the greedy algorithm and argue whether the result is optimal.
outline: χ(Kₙ) = n; χ(Cₙ) = 2 for even n and 3 for odd n; χ(bipartite with an edge) = 2.
Greedy colouring in any vertex order uses at most Δ + 1 colours.
Greedy can be suboptimal: give an ordering that wastes a colour on a bipartite graph.
Lower bound argument: a clique of size k forces χ ≥ k; odd cycles force χ ≥ 3.
Application: exam timetabling, register allocation, map colouring with four colours.

bank.q: For a given connected graph, find all bridges and all cut vertices, and identify the connected components left after removing a named vertex.
outline: Bridge test: an edge is a bridge iff it lies on no cycle.
Cut vertex test: v is a cut vertex iff removing v increases the number of components.
Worked removal of each candidate vertex, listing the resulting components.
Relation: a bridge that is not a pendant edge has endpoints that are cut vertices.
Application: single points of failure in a communication network.

bank.q: Prove that a connected graph has an Euler circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree, and use the result to discuss the route-inspection problem for a road network with odd-degree junctions.
outline: Necessity: each visit to a vertex uses one entering and one leaving edge.
Sufficiency: start anywhere and walk until stuck; the closed trail must use all edges of the component, otherwise a vertex on the trail has unused edges and an odd count.
Hierholzer's algorithm builds the circuit in O(|E|).
For odd-degree vertices, the Chinese postman problem duplicates edges along shortest paths between odd vertices.
Application: garbage collection, snow ploughing, post delivery routes.

bank.q: Compare Dijkstra's algorithm with Bellman-Ford. Explain with a small graph why Dijkstra fails when a negative edge weight is present, and state the running times of both.
outline: Dijkstra settles a vertex permanently on the smallest tentative distance — valid only if no later path can be shorter.
Negative edge counterexample: a settled vertex can later be improved.
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges |V| − 1 times, O(|V||E|), and detects negative cycles.
Dijkstra: O((|V| + |E|) log |V|) with a heap, O(|V|²) with an array.
All-pairs option: Floyd-Warshall O(|V|³).

bank.q: Prove that K₅ and K₃,₃ are non-planar using Euler's formula and the degree-of-faces bound, and discuss the consequences for planarity testing and map colouring.
outline: Bound |E| ≤ 3|V| − 6 fails for K₅: 10 > 9.
Triangle-free refinement |E| ≤ 2|V| − 4 rules out K₃,₃: 9 > 8.
Kuratowski's theorem: planar iff no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃.
Consequence: planarity is testable in linear time; non-planar drawings need crossings.
Map colouring: planar graphs are 4-colourable; the four colour theorem, and the earlier five colour theorem proof by induction on faces.

bank.q: Prove that every connected graph has a spanning tree, state the cut property of minimum weight edges, and use it to justify Kruskal's algorithm.
outline: Existence: repeatedly delete an edge on a cycle until no cycle remains; connectivity is preserved.
Cut property: for any cut, a minimum weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST.
Exchange argument: swapping a heavier edge for the light one keeps a spanning tree and does not increase weight.
Kruskal adds the lightest edge that crosses the cut between two components, so each choice is safe.
Conclusion: greedy is optimal; the number of MST edges is always |V| − 1.

glossary.def: A point or node of a graph, usually drawn as a dot and labelled v₁, v₂, …
A link between two vertices; written {u, v} when undirected and (u, v) when directed.
An edge that joins a vertex to itself.
A graph with no loops and no parallel edges.
A graph in which two vertices may be joined by more than one edge.
A graph whose edges are ordered pairs, so each edge has a direction from tail to head.
A graph whose vertex set and edge set are subsets of those of the original graph.
A sequence of vertices and edges v₀e₁v₁e₂…eₖvₖ; k is its length.
A closed walk of length at least 3 with no repeated vertices except the first and last.
Vertex v is reachable from u if some path leads from u to v.
In a digraph, every vertex is reachable from every other vertex following edge directions.
An acyclic graph; each of its connected components is a tree.
A vertex of degree 1 in a tree.
A region of the plane bounded by edges in a crossing-free drawing of a planar graph, including the unbounded outer face.
An assignment of colours to vertices in which no two adjacent vertices share a colour.
A set of vertices in which every pair is joined by an edge; a clique of size k forces at least k colours.
A subgraph that is a tree and contains every vertex of the original graph.
A partition of the vertex set into two non-empty parts; the edges crossing it are cut edges.
A graph in which every edge carries a number, such as distance in km or cost in rupees.
A data structure that returns the smallest stored key quickly; Dijkstra uses it to pick the next vertex.
A graph is bipartite iff it contains no odd cycle, which a breadth-first two-colouring detects.
A method that makes the best-looking choice at each step and never undoes it; correct for MST, not for Hamiltonian cycles.
The graph on the same vertices with an edge exactly where the original has none.
Σ deg(v) = 2|E| for every undirected graph.
The length of the shortest cycle in a graph that has one.
A property preserved by isomorphism, such as the number of vertices, edges or components.
